:::{.callout-note title="Overview"}
In this lecture, we focus on *practices* or how we can proceed to implement effective visualizations. We look at how to:

1. Ask yourself the critical questions that will help you to figure out what you need to do
2. Understand your development of visualizations in relation to the needs of your audience, and the essential challenges of visualizing variability and uncertainty
3. Combine your creative thinking with the flexibility of the Grammar of Graphics to produce effective plots.

You can navigate to each in the side bar on the right.
:::

#### Linked resources {#sec-7142-vis-lectures-out-links}

In a [linked lecture in PSYC7143](../../PSYC7143/7143_w6_vis-perspectives.qmd#sec-7143-w6-lectures), we look at *perspectives* or how we can think about visualization.

We look at:

  - Recent history –-- a selective sketch
  - Important case studies –-- a discussion
  - Identify your goals –-- a tool kit
  - Think about your audience --– a tool kit

There is a little repetition if you compare the two lectures because I do not assume you must view the practices lecture to understand the perspectives lecture. 

In the [linked tutorial in PSYC7142](./visualization.qmd#sec-vis-aims), we provide in-depth explanation of development processes and code steps that you can follow-up if you want to learn more about developing and producing visualizations for discovery and communication.

### Interactive lecture -- We work out how to build visualizations {#sec-7142-vis-lectures-lecture} 

You can watch the lecture videos using the playback windows shown next. The lecture is broken into three parts.

1. **Key questions for effective practice**
2. **Visualization development as a reflective process**
3. **Creativity times Grammar of Graphics for good practice**

::: callout-tip
During the lecture, I suggest some questions you can think about. Reflecting on your responses to these questions will help you to learn.
:::

You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.

The slides end with a references list but don't worry about reading what's in the references list, we give you recommended readings in @sec-7142-vis-reading.

::: callout-tip
The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: `visualisation-practices.html`. 

- [Lecture slides](files/visualisation-practices.html)

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.
:::

Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in sequence.

1. **Key questions for effective practice** (~13 minutes). Identifying the questions you need to ask yourself so that you can figure out what you need to do, and how and why you need to do it: What are our goals: discovery or communication? What is it our job to do? Where or when are we in the process? What investment is warranted?

2. **Visualization development as a reflective process** (~22 minutes). When you produce your visualization, you will need to ask yourself: Who is my audience and what do they need from my visualization? What are the sources of variability or uncertainty relevant to my job or my audience? What is my development process?

## Reading {#sec-7142-vis-reading}

::: {.callout-tip title="Easy access to readings"}
All reading is accessible via the library.

- **Essential**: We expect you to be familiar with these reading. You will be assessed on this.
- **Recommended**: We highly recommend these readings. They often provide a different perspective, or explain things in a different way.
- **Optional**: Further readings for those interested.
:::

This week, the reading is optional but **Recommended**:

Franconeri, S. L., Padilla, L. M., Shah, P., Zacks, J. M., & Hullman, J. (2021). The Science of Visual Data Communication: What Works. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*, 22(3), 110–161. <https://doi.org/10.1177/15291006211051956> **Recommended**

Gelman, A., & Unwin, A. (2013). Infovis and Statistical Graphics: Different Goals, Different Looks. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*, 22(1), 2–28. <https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2012.761137> **Recommended**

There are many sources of information online that will help you to produce great visualizations. You can find helpful introductory chapters in this free onlinebook:

Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. (2026). *R for Data Science* (2e ed.). https://r4ds.hadley.nz
